Geometric Thinking can be defined a lot of ways, however a simple way to think helps me:

  • I take the maximum amount of concentration I am capable of, and I manage my tasks during times of intended productivity using a geometric scheduler. I will plan my activities in order to have a combination of the most efficient framework and the most benefit to any in-efficient areas.

  • I will provide an example of how I apply this to software development.

Normally in software development you will use an IDE which is an integrated editor which helps keep track of all the pieces of the software project. An IDE can be as simple as a glorified file manager/text editor to being a highly automated or system administrator-oriented management tool.

An IDE of some kind is generally mandatory when working with a group, especially any Corporate structure.

"Compile On the Fly" applications such as the majority of the interfaces you see on the WWW do not require any kind of IDE. For example I use bash scripts, the vi text editor, OpenSSH and a preferred terminal emulator to accomplish all my development. Where in an IDE you might have integration between your documentation and your Database Schema, I have just moved my DB Schema from a text file into an Open Office Spreadsheet.

Ok so there is the background, so what does geometric thinking have to do with using an IDE or not?

  • Geometric Thinking while you are learning a new concept can position you to exponentially increase your benefits from later activities.

Here are a list of considerations I have made at various times, relative to various projects, to decide what kind of development environment I wanted to set up:

? How many managers on the project ? How high is the manager/idiocy ratio and how many management pretty picture reports will we need to produce

Those are the most likely ones, but for the sake of this explanation let's assume this is a solo project so I only need to consider the following:

? Am I going to use this programming language again ? Is anyone else going to be reading my code ? How much do I need to manage the production server at the end? ? How many people on the project ? Where are my weaknesses relative to my activities here

So one by one I will explain how each of these factors entered into my decision to use my current mode of development:

? Am I going to use this programming language again

Yes, but mainly because I know it the best. I would prefer to use something different, but I will stick with this language for pure efficiency of development time. If I was learning a new language, that builds a case for using an IDE because of the helpful features they can have like autocompletion and more robust syntax highlighting/manipulation features.

? Is anyone else going to be reading my code

Not at this time, though it is assumed they will in the future. This caused me to use a spreadsheet for the DB Schema. What does this have to do with geometric thinking? When you are interacting with other people, often you need to be using common tools. By using a spreadsheet as part of ability to communicate I am practicing with that tool to improve my ability to use one later. For example lets say I am slammed busy after a successful IPO, and the new shareholders want some numbers from me. Since I have been using this same framework [the spreadsheet] to communicate with my team this entire time, I am efficiently using my time as I am learning more about the spreadsheet as I go. The consideration of how much time I can afford to spend learning this spreadsheet as opposed to my old text document needs to take into account schedule pressures and the fact that humans aren't good at multitasking. [A whole digression about how much time it takes to task switch between two text documents and the relative merits of data organization in the spreadsheet - but the result being that the spreadsheet should be updated/used only at certain times so it is not a component of multitasking with another development process]

? How much do I need to manage the production server at the end?

On this one that is all me, so instead of using a built-in debugger in the IDE, I am testing code on a test webserver so I can see all the real world errors and behaviors. I am monitoring the access & error log files of my own test webserver which is how I will be monitoring in production. A debugging-IDE would be faster, but I am learning a lot from this, both about the code [learning from sometimes less than helpful error messages] and about the server behavior.

? How many people on the project

At some point, every project needs an IDE

? Where are my weaknesses relative to my activities here

Some of the modern database hooks and high level languages have changed significantly from what I am used to. I can benefit most by having to type things out instead of letting autocomplete put them in. I'm launching an app which will has a public userbase instead of a private userbase, so all the 3rd-layer security features I am used to are now 1st & 2nd layer defenses. So I can benefit most from using a live webserver environment as opposed to a debugger or even a virtual machine.

To maximize the benefit of Geometric Thinking it is also important when your ability to concentrate has been exceeded and remove variables. If you do not practice removing variables from time to time it may become difficult to function when you are forced to.

The best analogy I can part with; If any of you play Strategy Games;

Geometric Thinking is maximizing your tech tree while maintaining a strong economy and large tactical presence. A huge economy with glaring vulnerabilities is just as useless as a tiny economy with Particle Accelerators and no birthrate. Geometric Thinking is incorporating the best way to accomplish the desired end result into each act along the way - and still finishing before your enemy does.

In other words, if I die before I finish the software, none of this was anything but a game.
